hints: Look at the far right of Fig. 2.1 where the curve flattens - what does that flat level tell you about the fastest rate trypsin can achieve?
walkthrough:
Find Where the Curve Levels Off**
Think of $V_{max}$ as the speed limit for the enzyme when it is working as fast as it possibly can. On the graph, look along the y-axis for rate of reaction and follow the curve to the right where it becomes horizontal.

Read the Plateau Value**
The curve rises then plateaus at about 3.4 on the y-axis. That plateau is $V_{max}$, so $V_{max} = 3.4 \text{ } \mu\text{M min}^{-1}$. Remember to include the full units from the y-axis.

hints: Start from your $V_{max}$ value - what is half of that rate, and why is that half-rate the key to finding $K_m$?
Draw a horizontal line at half $V_{max}$ across to the curve, then drop vertically down to the x-axis - what substrate concentration do you read off?
walkthrough:
Work Out Half $V_{max}$**
$K_m$ is defined as the substrate concentration that gives half of $V_{max}$. Using (a)(i): $\frac{1}{2} V_{max} = 3.4 / 2 = 1.7 \text{ } \mu\text{M min}^{-1}$. Showing this working earns credit even if the final reading is slightly off.

Read $K_m$ From the Graph**
Find $1.7$ on the y-axis, move across to the curve, then straight down to the x-axis for substrate concentration. You land at about $0.15 \text{ mM}$. That x-value is $K_m$, so $K_m = 0.15 \text{ mM}$.

hints: Split the curve in your mind into two regions - the steep rise on the left up to about 0.25 mM and the flattening on the right above about 0.45 mM.
At low substrate, think about how many free active sites are available - what happens to collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes as you add a little more substrate?
At high substrate, think the opposite way - what runs out first, substrate or enzyme, and what does that mean for free active sites?
Link each description to its explanation - steep rise means substrate is limiting, plateau means enzyme is limiting because all active sites are occupied.
walkthrough:
Describe and Explain the Steep Rise**
At low substrate concentrations up to about 0.25 mM, the rate rises steeply and is roughly proportional to substrate concentration. This is because plenty of active sites are free. Adding more substrate means more frequent collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so substrate concentration is the limiting factor.

Describe and Explain the Slowing and Plateau**
From about 0.25 mM the increase becomes less steep, then above about 0.45 mM further increase in substrate gives no further increase in rate - the curve plateaus at $V_{max}$. This is because almost all active sites are now occupied at any moment.

Identify the New Limiting Factor**
Once saturated, adding more substrate cannot increase collisions usefully because there are no free active sites to bind to. Now the fixed enzyme concentration is limiting, so rate stays at maximum.

Final answer: At low substrate up to ~0.25 mM, rate is proportional to substrate concentration as not all active sites occupied and substrate is limiting. At higher substrate, rate of increase slows then plateaus at $3.4 \text{ } \mu\text{M min}^{-1}$ above ~0.45 mM as all active sites occupied and enzyme concentration is limiting.

hints: Positions 57, 102 and 195 are far apart if you think of the chain stretched out in a line - so what must happen to the chain to bring them together in 3D?
Recall the level of protein structure that describes the overall 3D folding of a single polypeptide - which level creates the specific shape of an active site?
Think about what holds that folded shape in place - which parts of the amino acids interact to stabilise the fold?
walkthrough:
Folding Brings Distant Parts Together**
Primary structure is just the linear sequence. Histidine 57, aspartate 102 and serine 195 are far apart in that line, but the chain does not stay straight. It folds and coils in three dimensions.

Name the Tertiary Structure**
That precise overall 3D folding of one polypeptide is the tertiary structure. Folding loops the chain so regions that are distant in sequence end up side by side, creating a pocket that becomes the active site.

Stabilised by R-Group Interactions**
The fold is held in position by interactions between R groups, such as hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions. These lock the three key amino acids in exactly the right positions to work together in catalysis.

Final answer: The polypeptide chain folds / coils into its tertiary structure, held by interactions between R groups, bringing amino acids distant in primary structure close together in 3D to form the active site.

hints: Trypsin is a protease that catalyses hydrolysis of peptide bonds - what small molecule is always used up in a hydrolysis reaction?
walkthrough:
Recall What Hydrolysis Means**
Hydrolysis means breaking a bond by adding water across it. Trypsin breaks peptide bonds between amino acids, and for each bond broken one molecule of water is used as a reactant to provide -H and -OH to the two products.
